title: So You Wanna Go Fast? (fixture: redaction gate)

lead_insight.claim: A two-line change that removed a single unnecessary string allocation on a byte-to-string-then-map-lookup path increased a production messaging server's throughput by two million messages per second.
lead_insight.context: The speaker describes a contribution to the NATS messaging server that inlined a []byte-to-string conversion directly into a map lookup instead of using an intermediate string variable.
lead_insight.evidence: So recently, there are, a while ago I guess, there was a contribution made to Nats, which was like a small two line change, and ended up increasing the throughput of the server by like two million messages a second, and all it did was remove an unnecessary string allocation.
lead_insight.speaker: instructor

insights.claim: defer's overhead ballooned and then was dramatically improved in Go 1.2/1.3, crept back up again, and by the time of the talk had settled back to roughly the same ~40ns overhead as a mutex lock/unlock.
insights.context: Discussion of whether defer is still considered slow, a long-running community concern.
insights.evidence: I mean, it's, to start off with, the I was there's a lot of overhead, but then in like go one two and one three, it really improved dramatically, and it kind of crept back up a little bit, but today it's kind of back at where it was and go on three, which in this case, this is like with a mutex lock unlock, it's like 40 nanoseconds of overhead.
insights.speaker: instructor

insights.claim: A lock-free channel implementation was written and benchmarked but never merged into Go because the team wanted more justification for the added complexity relative to the performance gain.
insights.context: Reference to Dmitry Vyukov's lock-free channel implementation attempt.
insights.evidence: But there was Dmitriev ukhov had an implementation of lock free channels, it never made it in, and I think the go team was looking for further justification for the added complexity that brings.
insights.speaker: instructor

build_ideas.title: Escape-analysis detective toolkit
build_ideas.pitch: Build a small CLI that runs go test -gcflags with -m, -l, and -S across a pair of benchmark files and diffs the inlining and assembly output side by side.
build_ideas.you_will_learn: How to read Go compiler inlining decisions (-m), disable inlining (-l), and dump generated assembly (-S).

origin.evidence: So we can verify that with the dash M compiler flag of the GC flags, and sure enough, is two calls to sortable that number that are being in lined on line 84.

build_ideas.title: DIY distributed reader-writer mutex with cache-line padding
build_ideas.pitch: Implement a per-CPU sharded RWMutex from scratch in Go and benchmark it against sync.RWMutex at increasing core counts.
build_ideas.you_will_learn: How false sharing occurs at the cache-line level and how to fix it with structural padding.

origin.evidence: So this is called a big reader lock, by the way, this kind of distributed readwrite mutex, and as you can see, it scales a lot better in comparison to the readwrite mutex from the sync package.

agent_prompts.title: False-sharing reproduction and fix
agent_prompts.what_it_does: Writes a Go benchmark demonstrating false sharing between two concurrently-accessed struct fields, then fixes it with cache-line padding.
agent_prompts.prompt: Write a Go benchmark package that demonstrates CPU cache false sharing between two int64 struct fields, then fix it with padding and compare throughput.

origin.evidence: So they end up thrashing that cache line, and so by adding these unused fields, we basically push those into their own cache lines.

agent_prompts.title: Interface-vs-struct sort benchmark
agent_prompts.what_it_does: Generates two Go benchmark files sorting 10 million elements and reports the performance gap.
agent_prompts.prompt: Create a Go module with two benchmark files comparing sort.Interface implementations, one via a concrete struct and one via an interface wrapper.

origin.evidence: And then we soared a hundred million of these things, and the results are kind of surprising.
